Bangladesh hospital wards crowded as measles toll nears grim 1,000-child mark. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh’s deadliest measles outbreak in decades is nearing the grim milestone of 1,000 child deaths, as a devastating epidemic sweeps through the country and crowded hospital wards fill with struggling babies.

Cries of sick children and the hiss of oxygen machines fill the air at Dhaka’s Shishu Hospital, where Rima Akter keeps a vigil beside her nine-month-old son.

“Just an hour ago, a child died, and they wheeled him out in front of us,” 30-year-old Akter told AFP on Thursday.

“We saw two children die today.”

Akter’s son Sabit Haque is one of scores filling the children’s hospital’s measles wards.

At least 986 children have died since March, while suspected and confirmed cases have surged past 180,000, according to the latest health ministry figures.

Measles is highly contagious, spreading through coughs and sneezes, and has no specific treatment once caught.

Complications can include brain swelling and severe breathing problems.

Although anyone can catch the disease, young children are particularly vulnerable.

The South Asian nation of 170 million has rolled out a mass vaccination drive to combat the outbreak, but case numbers continue to climb.

More than 1,000 suspected cases are reported daily.

‘Very weak’

“I’ve been running to and from multiple hospitals since July to get my son the proper treatment,” said Sanjana Islam Modina, 19, cradling her six-month-old son Ayan, who has an oxygen tube fixed to his nose.

Small dark spots covered Ayan’s head, fading from the angry red rash left by measles.

He was first admitted to hospital with pneumonia in July, then contracted measles before finally securing a bed at the capital’s specialised children’s hospital in mid-August.

Ayan spent 15 days in intensive care, before improving enough to return to the dedicated measles ward.

The hospital currently has 101 children admitted with suspected or confirmed measles.

“His lungs were already very weak from the pneumonia, then with measles his breathing was affected more,” Modina told AFP, while trying to soothe her wailing baby.

“He’s been on oxygen constantly for the last five days.”

Most cases recorded in Bangladesh during the current outbreak have been among children aged between six months and five years.

Doctors say many of the children arriving at hospital are already critically ill, with malnutrition further weakening their ability to fight the virus.

Ayan has also been diagnosed as malnourished.

“The doctors gave my son a special milk specifically designed for malnourished children,” said Modina, wiping sweat from his tiny forehead.

‘Devastating’

The outbreak has exposed gaps in Bangladesh’s efforts to protect its youngest.

SM Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman for health, called the outbreak “devastating”.

Bangladesh had previously made major advances in vaccination against infectious diseases, but a measles drive planned for 2024 was delayed by the uprising that toppled former prime minister Sheikh Hasina.

Workers’ strikes and political instability delayed a 2025 campaign.

The country has since rolled out a mass vaccination drive to combat the outbreak, but the number of cases continues to climb.

“There was a gap of a significant number of children missing the doses,” Hyder said.

“Healthcare workers… are vaccinating these children to close the gap.”

Mahmudur Rahman, an epidemiologist and former director of the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR), said Bangladesh should consider a broader vaccination campaign to contain the outbreak.

Rahman said public awareness was also crucial, stressing preventive measures including isolating infected children, handwashing and the use of masks by caregivers.

Worried mother Akter needs no reminder of how quickly the sickness can spread.

“We are aware of how contagious this disease is; our son was first admitted for bronchitis,” she said.

“After being released, we had to come back for measles.”

Header image: Children receive treatment for measles, at Bangladesh Shishu Hospital & Institute in Dhaka on Sept 3, 2026. — AFP

item.title: Turning waste into opportunity. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The scale of Bangladesh’s tannery waste problem is troubling, but there is certainly an economic opportunity hidden within it that we would be remiss to overlook.
Experts estimate that properly processing tannery waste and turning it into value-added products could generate an additional Tk2,000-3,000 crore in annual revenue.
This is precisely the kind of opportunity Bangladesh should be pursuing: One that can simultaneously address an environmental crisis, create new industries, generate employment, and also strengthen an important export sector.
For years, tannery waste has largely been treated as something to be disposed of rather than a resource to be recovered, and the consequences have been severe: Poorly managed waste has contributed to pollution around the Savar Tannery Industrial Estate, adding further pressure to already struggling waterways.
At a time when our rivers are being overwhelmed by industrial and other forms of waste, continuing with such a linear approach is simply unsustainable.
Yet, the materials currently being discarded have considerable potential.
Collagen-rich waste can be converted into products such as gelatin, industrial tallow, bio-fertilizer, and leather board, while chrome shavings and other by-products can have applications ranging from capsule shells to other industrial materials.
Even treatment-plant sludge has reportedly been used to produce tiles and bricks.
What is needed now is a serious transition towards a circular economy -- which will require investment in waste-processing facilities, green financing, appropriate incentives, research and development, and stronger links between waste processors and markets.
The government must also address the industry's environmental compliance problems. Environmental protection and economic growth should not be presented as opposing objectives; in this case, they can reinforce one another.
The opportunity before us is clear: Instead of allowing tannery waste to become another burden on our rivers and communities, Bangladesh should turn it into a valuable resource. Doing so would be good environmental policy -- and smart economics.

Feeding our future. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We agree with the State Minister for Primary and Mass Education Bobby Hajjaj that providing midday meals to schoolchildren must be viewed as a right rather than an act of charity.
His remarks come at an important time, as Bangladesh seeks to improve both access to and the quality of primary education.
A child cannot be expected to concentrate on lessons while hungry, and for many children from low-income households, the meal received at school may be the most integral part of their daily nutrition.
A properly designed and implemented school feeding program can, therefore, do much more than put food on a plate: It can improve attendance, concentration, learning outcomes, and ultimately a child's prospects in life.
This is particularly important if the government's stated ambition is to ensure that no child remains out of school, and that every child receives a proper education.
Investment in classrooms and textbooks will only go so far if children arrive at school hungry or leave because their families cannot afford to meet their basic needs.
However, recognizing this as a right also means recognizing the government's responsibility to deliver it properly. There can be no room for substandard food, irregular supplies, wastage, or corruption.
Thus, the minister's warning that poor-quality or unsuitable food will not be accepted is welcome.
Transparency and accountability must be built into every stage of the program, from procurement and transportation to distribution at individual schools. Teachers, parents and local communities should have meaningful avenues to monitor what children are receiving, and report irregularities.
Most importantly, the program must be expanded carefully and sustainably so that children across the country, regardless of where they live or their family's financial circumstances, can benefit.
A midday meal should never be something a child has to feel grateful for. It is an investment in their health, education and future -- and, by extension, in Bangladesh's future.

item.title: The power of thinking and questioning. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
More than three centuries ago, French philosopher René Descartes coined the famous phrase Cogito, ergo sum (I think, therefore I am) to define the essence of human existence.
His statement suggests that our ability to think is what makes us conscious, aware, and uniquely human. Because of the ability to think, human beings are often regarded as the most intelligent creatures on Earth.
Yet an important question remains: How many of us truly think, and how many think effectively?
In today's fast-paced world, there is a fine line between thinking and overthinking. Unfortunately, whenever someone pauses to analyze an issue deeply, question assumptions, or explore different possibilities, they are often labeled an “overthinker.”
As a result, many people become hesitant to ask questions or challenge conventional ideas.
However, progress has never come from unquestioned acceptance. Every invention, discovery, and social transformation began when someone dared to think differently and ask a simple but powerful question: “Why?”
Innovation is not merely about creating new technology; it is about developing new ways of understanding and solving problems. In a world facing increasingly complex challenges, the ability to think critically and question intelligently is a necessity.
If we look around Bangladesh, we will find no shortage of crises.
Every monsoon, floods affect millions of people, disrupting education, livelihoods, and communication.
In our cities, traffic congestion consumes valuable hours that could otherwise be spent on productive activities.
Plastic waste blocks drainage systems, contributing to urban flooding, while environmental pollution continues to threaten public health.
These problems are often discussed, criticized, and debated. Yet meaningful solutions emerge only when people move beyond complaints and begin asking the right questions.
Take the issue of urban flooding. Instead of merely blaming heavy rainfall, an innovative mind asks: Why do roads remain submerged long after the rain stops? Are drainage systems inadequate? Is unmanaged waste preventing water from flowing properly?
Such questions encourage us to investigate root causes rather than visible symptoms. Once the causes are identified, practical solutions become easier to design, whether through improved waste management, better urban planning, or community awareness campaigns.
Similarly, traffic congestion is not simply a transportation problem; it is also a thinking problem.
Every day, thousands of people lose valuable time on the roads. But what if students, engineers, and policy-makers worked together to rethink public transportation? What if technology could be used to monitor traffic flow more efficiently? What if flexible working hours reduced rush-hour pressure?
Progress begins when people challenge the assumption that existing conditions are unavoidable.
The same principle applies to education. Many students in remote areas still face barriers to quality learning. Rather than accepting this reality, innovators ask how digital technologies, community-based learning initiatives, or low-cost educational resources can bridge the gap.
Every educational advancement begins with someone identifying a problem and refusing to believe that it cannot be solved.
Innovation is not limited to laboratories, scientists, or large corporations. It begins with observation. It grows through curiosity. It develops through questioning.
A student who wonders how to reduce food waste in the cafeteria, save electricity in classrooms, or improve the campus environment is already thinking like an innovator.
The goal is not simply to find answers but to cultivate the habit of asking meaningful questions.
As Bangladesh moves toward a future shaped by rapid technological advancement and global challenges, the country will need more than skilled workers. It will need critical thinkers, problem-solvers, and innovators.
The next breakthrough idea may not come from a famous inventor or a multinational company. It may come from a student who dares to ask a question that others overlook.
Thinking is not a luxury but a responsibility. Questioning is not a sign of weakness but the beginning of wisdom. Every crisis carries within it an opportunity for innovation.
The moment we stop accepting problems as permanent and start questioning them, we take the first step toward meaningful change.
After all, every great solution begins with a simple question: “What if there is a better way?”
Md Inzamul Haque is a lecturer at the Department of English, Southeast University.

item.title: On the road again. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Travel has lost some of its old appeal in the global age, aided by instantaneous internet communication and the relative ease of travelling long distances.
In the old days, travel had a special meaning, particularly when the destination was a faraway country and the journey itself involved flying across continents.
Globalization, we are told, has killed distance. These days, hardly any place seems truly far away. Internet-mediated communication has also, in a sense, diminished culture shock.
Whether viscerally, in person, or virtually, we have already seen so much of the world. We can watch its streets, its people, its food, its politics and its landscapes on our screens.
Yet travelogue is not dead yet.
It is the unexpected encounters and experiences for which we are rarely prepared that make travelling worthwhile.
Zadar: Where nature plays music
In Zadar, an ancient Croatian city on the Adriatic coast, we encountered something that could hardly be experienced through a computer screen: The Sea Organ.
Built into the waterfront, it produces music through the movement of the waves. The sea itself becomes the musician.
As the waves enter the organ's pipes, they generate sounds that rise and fall unpredictably. Nearby, the Sun Salutation -- another remarkable installation -- responds to sunlight with a different kind of spectacle.
Between the sea, the sunset and the installations, Zadar offers something close to a symphony of nature and human creativity.
The waves of the Adriatic not only catch the eye; they soothe the ear.
That is perhaps what travel does best. It brings together things that we may know intellectually but have never actually experienced.
Education, sport, and Croatia
We attended a workshop at the University of Zadar, an institution that goes back to 1396, one of the oldest universities in East Europe.
Later, we met members of the city council. Their offices were decorated with large posters of famous Croatian football stars. It was football season, and the national team was very much on people's minds.
I asked a simple question: How does a country of fewer than four million people repeatedly produce athletes capable of competing at the highest level of international sport?
Football, of course, is only part of the story. Croatia has also produced world-class athletes in tennis, skiing, rowing, water polo, handball, athletics, and other sports. The country's sporting achievements are remarkable relative to its small population.
Sport is taken seriously as part of children's education and community life. Croatia has a national sports program that explicitly links sport with the educational system and sets responsibilities for national and local authorities, while its education system includes physical education and opportunities for students to pursue sport more intensively.
The idea that education, sport, music, and community life could be treated as complementary components of a child's development struck me.
Migrants far from home
Croatia also has experienced a significant increase in foreign workers, including workers from Nepal who are quite visible. Bangladeshis were present too though in much smaller numbers.
I had conversations with Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia during their work breaks. They seemed pleasantly surprised that people they described as bhadralok -- people from the educated and relatively privileged sections of society -- would simply stop and talk to them on the sidewalk.
Many described precarious lives: Insecure employment, uncertain immigration status, and limited social support.
One worker told me something that stayed with me. When ministers and senior officials from Dhaka visited Malaysia, he said, they often met Bengali businesspeople, community leaders, and embassy officials but had little time to meet the ordinary workers whose remittances make such an important contribution to Bangladesh's economy.
I wondered: Why should it be so difficult to talk to the people who do some of the hardest work and whose earnings contribute so substantially to the country's foreign-exchange reserves?
Perhaps governments everywhere need to remember that migrants are not merely sources of remittances. They are citizens, workers, and human beings whose experiences provide an important measure of how a country values its people.
Australia: Democracy and the welfare state
In Australia, I spent some quiet time at the Museum of Australian Democracy at Old Parliament House in Canberra.
The building was Australia's federal Parliament from 1927 until 1988, when Parliament moved to the new Parliament House on Capital Hill. In 2009, the old building became the home of the Museum of Australian Democracy.
Walking through the museum was an encounter with Australia's political memory. I came across displays devoted to former prime ministers, including references to their education and careers.
Among them was Robert -- Bob -- Hawke, whom I had briefly encountered in Adelaide in 2015. Hawke, then in a wheelchair, appeared at a conference I was attending. He came to our session, and I had the opportunity to shake his hand and exchange a few words with him.
When I met him, I reminded him that I had been a graduate student in the United States when he became prime minister and had read about his life in The New York Times. That was how I knew about his Rhodes Scholarship.
He seemed pleased that I remembered it. But I had the impression that, for Hawke, being a Rhodes Scholar was not what defined his life.
His real accomplishments, in his own eyes, were his leadership of the trade union movement and his service as prime minister.
That distinction is worth remembering. Education can open doors, but what a person does with that education is ultimately more important than the credential itself.
Australia also offers an interesting example of the welfare state in everyday life.
Habibul Haque Khondker is a sociologist and columnist.

item.title: Ninth national pay scale: The real test. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Public employees deserve fair wages. But a government pay scale is never only about government employees.
When millions of households are already struggling with high prices, weak purchasing power, and economic uncertainty, a large public-sector wage increase inevitably becomes a question of wider economic justice.
That is why the approval of the ninth national pay scale deserves to be examined not simply as a salary revision, but as a major macro-economic policy decision.
The new pay structure raises basic salaries by up to 142%, with the minimum basic salary rising to Tk20,000 and the maximum to Tk1,56,000. Full implementation is expected to require an additional Tk106,000 crore annually.
The question is not whether government employees deserve better pay. They do. The harder question is: How can Bangladesh implement such a large wage adjustment without making life even more expensive for everyone else?
Bangladesh is entering this reform with little room for complacency. Headline inflation stood at 8.32% in July 2026, while non-food inflation remained higher at 9.28%. The average inflation rate for FY2025–26 was 8.68%.
For a salaried household, these numbers are not abstract economic indicators. They mean that the same income buys less food, transport, education, healthcare, and other necessities than it did before.
And the burden is not evenly distributed.
According to the latest Labour Force Survey 2024, around 84% of employed people -- approximately 5.80 crore workers -- are engaged in informal employment.
These workers do not receive a government pay revision every few years. Many have no automatic cost-of-living adjustment, no guaranteed annual increment, and limited protection against sudden price increases.
This creates the central distributional dilemma of pay scale: A wage increase for millions of public employees can be justified, but who protects the millions who have no employer capable of passing higher costs on to someone else?
Of course, the pay scale alone will not cause Bangladesh’s inflation. That would be economically simplistic. Inflation has multiple drivers -- exchange rates, food supply, import costs, energy prices, market concentration, fiscal and monetary conditions, and global commodity shocks.
But a major wage-driven increase in aggregate demand can add pressure when supply-side constraints are already severe.
The transmission mechanism is straightforward:
Government wages rise → consumption rises → prices respond → private employees demand higher wages → business costs increase → investment and competitiveness suffer → inflationary pressure persists.
This concern is not simply theoretical. Business leaders have already warned that higher public-sector wages could increase pressure on the private sector, particularly labour-intensive industries already struggling with energy shortages, high borrowing costs, and an unstable business environment.
If private employers respond by raising wages, they may also face higher production costs. If they cannot absorb those costs, prices may rise. If they cannot raise prices because of weak demand or international competition, investment and employment may suffer.
This is where Bangladesh needs to look beyond the government payroll.
The latest external economic outlook is hardly reassuring. The World Bank has projected Bangladesh’s FY2025–26 growth at only 3.9%, citing elevated inflation, weak investment, financial-sector vulnerabilities, and the effects of the Middle East conflict.
It has also warned that poverty has already increased and that further shocks could push more people below the poverty line.
Recent shocks have pushed up international prices of energy and agricultural inputs, with crude oil, LNG, and nitrogen fertilizer prices all experiencing significant increases.
For Bangladesh, this matters enormously. Higher energy and fertilizer costs eventually reach farmers, transport operators, manufacturers, and consumers.
The agricultural economy is particularly vulnerable. According to FAO, around 10 lakh agricultural households -- nearly 50 lakh people -- are projected to need emergency agricultural assistance during June-November 2026.
These numbers should force a broader question: While the state increases the purchasing power of public employees, what is the state’s plan for protecting the purchasing power of everyone else?
At present, Bangladesh’s social safety-net system is not designed to function as a universal shield against inflation. Informal workers, low-income households, small producers, and many private-sector employees remain highly exposed to economic shocks.
A pay scale without a parallel protection strategy risks creating a two-speed economy: One group receives an institutionalized income adjustment, while another absorbs the consequences through higher prices and weaker real wages.
That would be economically inefficient and socially unfair.
What should be done?
First, establish a pay scale-inflation monitoring framework. The government should monitor the impact of the new pay structure on inflation, consumption, private-sector wages, employment, and fiscal sustainability.
If inflationary pressures intensify significantly, subsequent phases of implementation should be reviewed rather than treated as automatic.
Second, protect workers beyond the public payroll. Temporary, targeted income support should be expanded for low-income informal workers and vulnerable households during periods of severe inflation. Social protection must become more responsive to economic shocks rather than functioning mainly as a collection of static programs.
Third, address the supply side. Wage reform cannot be separated from food security, energy reliability, fertilizer availability, import management, and market competition. If supply cannot respond to rising demand, wage increases will translate too easily into higher prices.
Fourth, finance the pay scale through structural reform rather than excessive fiscal pressure. Stronger domestic revenue mobilization, better tax compliance, expenditure rationalization, and improved public financial management are essential. Borrowing simply to finance recurrent wage and pension commitments would shift today's adjustment costs onto tomorrow's taxpayers.
Finally, Bangladesh must stop viewing wage policy, inflation policy, and social protection as separate policy silos. They are deeply interconnected.
A government employee struggling to pay rent and educate children deserves a decent salary.
But so does the garment worker whose wage does not automatically rise with inflation.
So does the rickshaw puller whose daily income is uncertain.
So does the small farmer face higher fertilizer and fuel costs.
So does the informal worker who has no pension, no paid leave, and no protection against economic shocks.
The real measure of the ninth national pay scale should therefore not be how much government employees receive on their pay slips. It should be whether Bangladesh can raise public-sector incomes without reducing the real incomes of millions outside the public sector.
The government has an opportunity to demonstrate that wage reform and economic stability do not have to be opposing goals. But that needs more than a new salary structure.
It requires a coherent macroeconomic strategy that manages inflation, protects vulnerable workers, strengthens supply chains, and ensures that fiscal reform is sustainable.
A pay rise for some should not become a price rise for everyone. That is the real test.
Amith Kumar Malaker is a human rights defender and public policy analyst based in Bangladesh.

item.title: Govt should end extortion, prowl of intermediaries. [ newagebd ]
item.description: BUSINESS leaders and market analysts as well as traders have put goods prices increase down to rampant extortion and unchecked dominance of intermediaries, noting that there is no scope for prices to increase if the supply remains smooth. This is not the first time that they have made such observations. They earlier did, perhaps one group at a time. But this time they...
